doc.title: Sam Kininger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 27, 2011

title: Playing outside the chord; Kenny Garrett's phrasing
summary: Rowe asks about an outside phrase on a YouTube clip; Sam explains chromatic outside playing and returning home.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I was looking at one of theYouTube clips of you last night and it was with Soulive I think, and I think the tune was “Right On”? © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-
“Right On.”
Okay. So down below there’s all these comments people make.
Um hum.

And the guy, someone wrote “what is Sam playing at 4:07?” The guy had timed the thing, and I said well I’m going to listen to this. And sure enough, when it got to 4:07 you played something that was out of the chord so to speak.
Oh okay.
So shall we say “outside.”
Right. Yeah I do that a lot, yeah.
So how do I ask this? Do you have things in your head that you know you can go to?

Sort of, yeah. Well I guess it’s like finding your way home, is the best way I can figure of explaining. Like if you’re in one chord like F say for example, you know a lot of people, you know you can go a half step above F, a half step below F, while you’re soloing [scats] you know and just resolve it. So maybe that’s what he’s hearing? It sounds different when you’re in that jam situation, you know what I mean? Because it’s not like a jazz progression but I’m playing over that change. In my mind I’m playing kind of over a different change and kind of creating other chords, but then it all comes back to one, if that makes sense.
Sure. Does it — because theoretically those could be called “wrong notes.”
Yeah.
So how do you make them right?
You’re only a half step away, right, from the right note? Someone said that to me once.
Yeah. Okay.

But I play a lot chromatically. I play, obviously rhythmic things and then it’s just fun to go outside of just playing and it definitely stimulates your mind and it forces you to think while you’re playing too, and it’s like how do I get back to this place? You know?
No, that’s very well said. Because you probably would never end your solo being a half step away from where you should be.
[scats] No, you’ve got to get back to F. I do a lot of that though I guess. I don’t know what the word is for it, but yeah.
Playing outside, coming back.
You ever check out Kenny Garrett?
Um hum.
He does, a lot of his phrasing is like that. So check him out. He definitely influenced my style of playing.
